steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing FIRE, a functional relative positional encoding with progressive interpolation for length generalization in decoder-only Transformer language models. Motivate the length generalization problem, review existing position encodings, explain the method and experiments at a high level, and end with a bulleted contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Long-context applications vs. poor length generalization of Transformer LMs
2. Position encodings and why they fail to generalize
3. Our approach: FIRE (learnable function + progressive interpolation)
4. Two extra transformations (log, learnable threshold)
5. Experiments overview
6. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- Transformer LMs: SOTA zero-shot on many NLP tasks -> longer context applications: chat bots, long document summarization, QA
- accuracy drops quickly for inputs longer than training length; training inputs short (e.g. 2048 for LLaMA) to avoid quadratic attention cost
- interest in length generalization: train short (e.g. 2048), test long (e.g. 8192)

2. Position encodings
- Transformers permutation equivariant, agnostic to ordering -> rely on position encodings
- APE, RoPE: don't generalize beyond training lengths
- T5's relative PE: generalizes (same representation for all OOD lengths) but slow vector ops on modern accelerators
- other work: inductive biases on how attention decays with length
- recent: no position encodings in decoder-only models -> better length generalization, only small-scale synthetic tasks

3. FIRE
- functional approach to learn relative position biases, not hard-coded inductive biases; decoder-only focus
- FIRE = Functional Interpolation for Relative Positional Encoding
- i) learnable function maps positions to biases; ii) progressive interpolation -> bounded input for all sequence lengths
- functional => adapts to task rather than fixed bias (e.g. towards nearby tokens)
- MLP; theory: can represent T5's RPE, Alibi, Kerple parameter-efficiently; tiny MLP hidden size 32, accelerator-friendly
- progressive interpolation: normalize query-key relative distance by query position; causal attention -> distance between 0 and query position -> output bounded between 0 and 1
- longer sequences -> progressively finer grids, interpolating the function

4. Transformations
- locality bias: \log transformation of relative distance before MLP; amplifies differences for local tokens
- learnable threshold in normalizer -> exact distances for shorter contexts
- neither limits learning arbitrary biases; some heads attend more to far away contexts

5. Experiments
- language modeling: C4, arXiv, Github; SCROLLS; zero-shot long-context QA (NarrativeQA); GLUE/SuperGLUE
- strong length generalization + long text modeling; competitive on short tasks
- visualization: diverse patterns beyond locality bias

6. Contributions
- FIRE: functional relative PE; progressive interpolation -> bounded domain, then learned mapping
- theory: represents T5's RPE, Alibi, Kerple -> unifies class of approaches
- empirical: zero-shot + finetuning; C4: beats best baseline by 2.28 perplexity points (Fig. 1); SCROLLS: over 1 point on average (Table 1)
- visualization: local and anti-local biases

But the accuracy of these models usually drops quickly when the inputs are longer than the ones used in training, and the training inputs are usually fairly short (e.g. 2048 for LLaMA) so that the expensive quadratic attention cost during training is avoided. Because of this there has been significant interest in improving length generalization of Transformers, where the model is trained on shorter inputs (e.g. 2048) and then its performance is tested on longer inputs (e.g. 8192).

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Transformer based Language Models have shown state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on many natural language processing tasks, and this enables applications with longer and longer context, like chat bots and long document summarization and question answering. But the accuracy of these models usually drops quickly when the inputs are longer than the ones used in training, and the training inputs are usually fairly short (e.g. 2048 for LLaMA) so that the expensive quadratic attention cost during training is avoided. Because of this there has been significant interest in improving length generalization of Transformers, where the model is trained on shorter inputs (e.g. 2048) and then its performance is tested on longer inputs (e.g. 8192).

Transformers are fundamentally permutation equivariant and don't care about the ordering of the input sequence. They need position encodings to learn the order of the input tokens. Popular position encodings like Absolute Positional Encoding (APE) and the more recent Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE) don't generalize to contexts longer than the ones seen in training. T5's relative positional encoding does generalize to longer contexts because it uses the same representation for all out of distribution (OOD) sequence lengths, but it has slow vector operations on modern accelerators. Another line of recent work encourages length generalization by encoding specific inductive biases about how attention should decay with sequence length. More recently, some authors show that using no position encodings in decoder-only models can give better length generalization, although only for small-scale synthetic tasks.

In this work we use a functional approach to learn the relative position biases, instead of hard coding inductive biases, with the goal of training language models that generalize in length (we focus on decoder-only models). We propose the FIRE (Functional Interpolation for Relative Positional Encoding) method, which i) uses a learnable function to map the input positions to biases, and ii) uses a progressive interpolation technique that makes sure the input to the position encoding function is bounded for all input sequence lengths, and this is what enables length generalization.

Learning the biases with a functional approach lets the model adapt to the task at hand instead of always having the same inductive bias, e.g. a bias towards nearby tokens as in prior methods. Specifically we use an MLP to learn the biases, and we prove theoretically that it can represent several popular methods like T5's RPE, Alibi, and Kerple in a parameter efficient way. Actually all our experiments use a tiny MLP with a hidden size of 32, which is also friendly to accelerators, unlike T5's RPE. Next, our progressive interpolation technique normalizes the query-key relative distance by the query position. For causal attention in language models the relative distance is always between 0 and the query position, so progressive interpolation gives an output that is always bounded between 0 and 1. So the input to the position encoding function is bounded for all input sequence lengths, which leads to better generalization performance. As a result, as the sequence lengths get longer and longer, the positional inputs form finer and finer grids, interpolating the positional encoding function on the interval from 0 to 1.

Inspired by existing methods, we add the following two transformations to FIRE, which we found help improve the model quality. i) To encourage a locality bias in FIRE, we apply the popular \log transformation to the relative distance before it goes into the MLP, which amplifies the input differences for local tokens. ii) Then we modify progressive interpolation with a learnable threshold in the normalizer so that it gives exact distances for shorter contexts. Note that neither of these transformations limits the ability of the model to learn arbitrary biases. In fact we show that FIRE learns to pay more attention to far away contexts in some attention heads.

We do an extensive empirical study to show that FIRE is effective for length generalization. We benchmark FIRE and other positional encoding approaches on a wide range of real-world language modeling (C4, arXiv, and Github), a long text benchmark (SCROLLS), zero-shot long-context question answering (NarrativeQA), and natural language understanding benchmarks (GLUE/SuperGLUE). The empirical results show strong length generalization performance and long text modeling capability of FIRE. Our experiments on standard natural language understanding benchmarks show that FIRE is competitive on short sequence tasks too. We also visualize the learned positional encoding of FIRE and show that it learns diverse patterns, not only locality bias.

The main contributions of our paper are:

- We propose FIRE, a new functional relative positional encoding method. With progressive interpolation, FIRE can transform arbitrary input lengths into a bounded domain, and then a learned mapping is applied.

- We prove theoretically that FIRE can represent popular position encodings like T5's RPE, Alibi, and Kerple, so it unifies a class of existing position encoding approaches.

- We show empirically that FIRE has strong length generalization behavior and improves significantly over existing methods in zero-shot and finetuning settings on a wide range of datasets and benchmarks. For example, it consistently gives the strongest performance on C4 language modeling across various sequence lengths and beats the best baseline by 2.28 perplexity points (Fig. 1). On the SCROLLS long text benchmark, FIRE beats all competing methods on average by over 1 point (Table 1).

- We visualize the learned position embeddings of the FIRE model and show that it can learn both local and anti-local position biases.

We conduct an extensive empirical study to demonstrate the effectiveness of FIRE for length generalization, benchmarking FIRE and other positional encoding approaches on a wide range of real-world language modeling (C4, arXiv, and Github), long text benchmark (SCROLLS), zero-shot long-context question answering (NarrativeQA), and natural language understanding benchmarks (GLUE/SuperGLUE). Our empirical results show the strong length generalization performance and long text modeling capability of FIRE, and our experiments on standard natural language understanding benchmarks show that FIRE is competitive on short sequence tasks as well. We further visualize the learned positional encoding of FIRE, showing that it learns diverse patterns beyond just locality bias.

The main contributions of our paper are summarized below:

- We propose FIRE, a new functional relative positional encoding method. Using progressive interpolation, FIRE transforms arbitrary input lengths into a bounded domain, followed by a learned mapping.

- We theoretically prove that FIRE can represent popular position encodings such as T5's RPE, Alibi, and Kerple, thereby unifying a class of existing position encoding approaches.

- We empirically show the strong length generalization behavior of FIRE, which significantly improves over existing methods in zero-shot and finetuning settings on a wide range of datasets and benchmarks. For instance, it consistently delivers the strongest performance on C4 language modeling across various sequence lengths, outperforming the best baseline by 2.28 perplexity points (Fig. 1). On the SCROLLS long text benchmark, FIRE surpasses all competing methods on average by over 1 point (Table 1).

- We present visualizations of the learned position embeddings of FIRE, showing that it can learn both local and anti-local position biases.
